# eeprom24x - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eeprom24x/

## Expand description

This is a platform agnostic Rust driver for the 24x series serial EEPROM,
based on the [ embedded-hal](https://github.com/rust-embedded/embedded-hal) traits.

This driver allows you to:

- Read a single byte from a memory address. See `read_byte()`
- Read a byte array starting on a memory address. See: `read_data()`
- Read the current memory address (please read notes). See: `read_current_address()`
- Write a byte to a memory address. See: `write_byte()`
- Write a byte array (up to a memory page) to a memory address. See: `write_page()`
- Read `CSx`-variant devices’ factory-programmed unique serial. See:`read_unique_serial()`
- Use the device in generic code via the `Eeprom24xTrait`

If an `embedded_hal::timer::CountDown` is available, the [ embedded-storage](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/embedded-storage) traits can
additionally be used which allow to read the device capacity and write over page boundaries. To
achieve the latter, the

[has to be wrapped with](https://docs.rs/struct.Eeprom24x.html)

`Eeprom24x`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Storage.html#method.new)

`Storage::new`Can be used at least with the devices listed below.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-devices)The devices

These devices provides a number of bits of serial electrically erasable and programmable read only memory (EEPROM) organized as a number of words of 8 bits each. The devices’ cascadable feature allows up to 8 devices to share a common 2-wire bus. The devices are optimized for use in many industrial and commercial applications where low power and low voltage operation are essential.

| Device | Memory bits | 8-bit words | Page size | Datasheet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24x00 | 128 bits | 16 | N/A | [24C00](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/24AA00-24LC00-24C00-Data-Sheet-20001178J.pdf) |
| 24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 8 bytes | [AT24C01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 16 bytes | [M24C01](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c01-r.pdf) |
| 24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 8 bytes | [AT24C02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 16 bytes | [M24C02](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c02-r.pdf) |
| 24x04 | 4 Kbit | 512 | 16 bytes | [AT24C04](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8896E-SEEPROM-AT24C04D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x08 | 8 Kbit | 1,024 | 16 bytes | [AT24C08](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/AT24C08D-I2C-Compatible-2-Wire-Serial-EEPROM-20006022A.pdf) |
| 24x16 | 16 Kbit | 2,048 | 16 bytes | [AT24C16](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/20005858A.pdf) |
| 24x32 | 32 Kbit | 4,096 | 32 bytes | [AT24C32](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x64 | 64 Kbit | 8,192 | 32 bytes | [AT24C64](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x128 | 128 Kbit | 16,384 | 64 bytes | [AT24C128](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8734-SEEPROM-AT24C128C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x256 | 256 Kbit | 32,768 | 64 bytes | [AT24C256](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8568-SEEPROM-AT24C256C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x512 | 512 Kbit | 65,536 | 128 bytes | [AT24C512](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8720-SEEPROM-AT24C512C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM01 | 1 Mbit | 131,072 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8812-SEEPROM-AT24CM01-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM02 | 2 Mbit | 262,144 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8828-SEEPROM-AT24CM02-Datasheet.pdf) |

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

[§](https://docs.rs#defmt-03)defmt-03

To enable [defmt](https://crates.io/crates/defmt) (version `0.3.x`) support, when specifying the dependency on `eeprom24x`, add the feature “`defmt-03`”.

```
[dependencies]
eeprom24x = { version = "0.7.2", features = ["defmt-03"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples-see-also-examples-folder)Usage examples (see also examples folder)

To create a new instance you can use the `new_<device>` methods.
There are many compatible vendors so the method has a somewhat generic name.
For example, if you are using an AT24C32, you can create a device by calling
`Eeprom24x::new_24x32(...)`.
Please refer to the [device table](https://docs.rs#the-devices) above for further examples
of device names.

Please find additional examples using hardware in this repository: [driver-examples](https://github.com/eldruin/driver-examples)

[§](https://docs.rs#instantiating-with-the-default-address)Instantiating with the default address

Import this crate and an `embedded_hal` implementation, then instantiate
the device:

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let address = SlaveAddr::default();
// using the AT24C256
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, address);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#providing-an-alternative-address)Providing an alternative address

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let (a2, a1, a0) = (false, false, true);
let address = SlaveAddr::Alternative(a2, a1, a0);
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, address);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#writing-and-reading-a-byte)Writing and reading a byte

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
let address = 0x1234;
let data = 0xAB;
eeprom.write_byte(address, data);
// EEPROM enters internally-timed write cycle. Will not respond for some time.
let retrieved_data = eeprom.read_byte(address);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#writing-a-page)Writing a page

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
let address = 0x1234;
let data = [0xAB; 64];
eeprom.write_page(address, &data);
// EEPROM enters internally-timed write cycle. Will not respond for some time.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-embedded-storage-traits)Using embedded-storage traits

```
use linux_embedded_hal::{I2cdev, Delay};
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr, Storage };
use embedded_storage::{ReadStorage, Storage as _};
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
let mut storage = Storage::new(eeprom, Delay {});
let _capacity = storage.capacity();
let address = 0x1234;
let data = [0xAB; 256];
storage.write(address, &data);
// EEPROM writes four pages. This introduces a delay of at least 20 ms, 5 ms per page.
```

# eeprom24x - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eeprom24x/0.7.2/eeprom24x/

## Expand description

This is a platform agnostic Rust driver for the 24x series serial EEPROM,
based on the [ embedded-hal](https://github.com/rust-embedded/embedded-hal) traits.

This driver allows you to:

- Read a single byte from a memory address. See `read_byte()`

- Read `CSx`-variant devices’ factory-programmed unique serial. See:`read_unique_serial()`
- Use the device in generic code via the `Eeprom24xTrait`

If an `embedded_hal::timer::CountDown` is available, the [ embedded-storage](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/embedded-storage) traits can

# eeprom24x 0.7.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/eeprom24x/latest

# Rust 24x EEPROM Driver

This is a platform agnostic Rust driver for the 24x series serial EEPROM,
based on the [ embedded-hal](https://github.com/rust-embedded/embedded-hal) traits.

This driver allows you to:

- Read a single byte from a memory address. See: `read_byte()`.
- Read a byte array starting on a memory address. See: `read_data()`.
- Read the current memory address (please read notes). See: `read_current_address()`.
- Write a byte to a memory address. See: `write_byte()`.
- Write a byte array (up to a memory page) to a memory address. See: `write_page()`.
- Read `CSx`-variant devices' factory-programmed unique serial. See:`read_unique_serial()`.
- Use the device in generic code via the `Eeprom24xTrait`.

Can be used at least with the devices listed below.

## The devices

These devices provides a number of bits of serial electrically erasable and programmable read only memory (EEPROM) organized as a number of words of 8 bits each. The devices' cascadable feature allows up to 8 devices to share a common 2-wire bus. The devices are optimized for use in many industrial and commercial applications where low power and low voltage operation are essential.

| Device | Memory bits | 8-bit words | Page size | Datasheet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24x00 | 128 bits | 16 | N/A | [24C00](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/24AA00-24LC00-24C00-Data-Sheet-20001178J.pdf) |
| 24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 8 bytes | [AT24C01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 16 bytes | [M24C01](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c01-r.pdf) |
| 24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 8 bytes | [AT24C02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 16 bytes | [M24C02](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c02-r.pdf) |
| 24x04 | 4 Kbit | 512 | 16 bytes | [AT24C04](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8896E-SEEPROM-AT24C04D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x08 | 8 Kbit | 1,024 | 16 bytes | [AT24C08](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/AT24C08D-I2C-Compatible-2-Wire-Serial-EEPROM-20006022A.pdf) |
| 24x16 | 16 Kbit | 2,048 | 16 bytes | [AT24C16](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/20005858A.pdf) |
| 24x32 | 32 Kbit | 4,096 | 32 bytes | [AT24C32](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x64 | 64 Kbit | 8,192 | 32 bytes | [AT24C64](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x128 | 128 Kbit | 16,384 | 64 bytes | [AT24C128](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8734-SEEPROM-AT24C128C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x256 | 256 Kbit | 32,768 | 64 bytes | [AT24C256](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8568-SEEPROM-AT24C256C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x512 | 512 Kbit | 65,536 | 128 bytes | [AT24C512](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8720-SEEPROM-AT24C512C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM01 | 1 Mbit | 131,072 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8812-SEEPROM-AT24CM01-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM02 | 2 Mbit | 262,144 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8828-SEEPROM-AT24CM02-Datasheet.pdf) |

## Usage

To use this driver, import this crate and an `embedded_hal` implementation,
then instantiate the appropriate device.
In the following examples an instance of the device AT24C256 will be created
as an example. Other devices can be created with similar methods like:
`Eeprom24x::new_24x64(...)`.

Please find additional examples using hardware in this repository: [driver-examples](https://github.com/eldruin/driver-examples)

```
use ;
use DelayMs;
use ;
```
## Features

### defmt-03

To enable [defmt](https://crates.io/crates/defmt) (version `0.3.x`) support, when specifying the dependency on `eeprom24x`, add the feature "`defmt-03`".

```
[]
 = {  = "0.7.2",  = ["defmt-03"] }
```

[issue in the github project](https://github.com/eldruin/eeprom24x-rs/issues).

                    eeprom24x 0.7.2

# embedded_hal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/embedded-hal/^1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#embedded-hal)`embedded-hal`

A Hardware Abstraction Layer (HAL) for embedded systems

This project is developed and maintained by the [HAL team](https://github.com/rust-embedded/wg#the-hal-team).

[§](https://docs.rs#companion-crates)Companion crates

The main `embedded-hal` crate contains only blocking traits, where the operation is done
synchronously before returning. Check out the following crates, which contain versions
of the traits for other execution models:

- `embedded-hal-async`
- `embedded-hal-nb`- `nb`crate.

The [ embedded-hal-bus](https://docs.rs/embedded-hal-bus) crate provides utilities for sharing
SPI and I2C buses.

Additionally, more domain-specific traits are available in separate crates:

- `embedded-can`
- `embedded-io`- `std::io`, but- `no-std`-compatible).

[§](https://docs.rs#serialuart-traits)Serial/UART traits

There is no serial traits in `embedded-hal`. Instead, use [ embedded-io](https://crates.io/crates/embedded-io).
A serial port is essentially a byte-oriented stream, and that’s what

`embedded-io` models. Sharing the traits
with all byte streams has some advantages. For example, it allows generic code providing a command-line interface
or a console to operate either on hardware serial ports or on virtual ones like Telnet or USB CDC-ACM.[§](https://docs.rs#design-goals)Design goals

The HAL

-
Must *erase*device specific details. Neither register, register blocks, nor magic values should appear in the API.
-
Must be generic *within*a device and*across*devices. The API to use a serial interface must be the same regardless of whether the implementation uses the USART1 or UART4 peripheral of a device or the UART0 peripheral of another device.
-
Where possible must *not*be tied to a specific asynchronous model. The API should be usable in blocking mode, with the`futures`model, with an async/await model or with a callback model. (cf. the`nb`
-
Must be minimal, and thus easy to implement and zero cost, yet highly composable. People that want higher level abstraction should *prefer to use this HAL*rather than*re-implement*register manipulation code.
-
Serve as a foundation for building an ecosystem of platform-agnostic drivers. Here driver means a library crate that lets a target platform interface an external device like a digital sensor or a wireless transceiver. The advantage of this system is that by writing the driver as a generic library on top of `embedded-hal`driver authors can support any number of target platforms (e.g. Cortex-M microcontrollers, AVR microcontrollers, embedded Linux, etc.). The advantage for application developers is that by adopting`embedded-hal`they can unlock all these drivers for their platform.
-
Trait methods must be fallible so that they can be used in any possible situation. Nevertheless, HAL implementations can additionally provide infallible versions of the same methods if they can never fail in their platform. This way, generic code can use the fallible abstractions provided here but platform-specific code can avoid fallibility-related boilerplate if possible.

[§](https://docs.rs#out-of-scope)Out of scope

- Initialization and configuration stuff like “ensure this serial interface and that SPI
interface are not using the same pins”. The HAL will focus on *doing I/O*.

[§](https://docs.rs#platform-agnostic-drivers)Platform agnostic drivers

You can find platform-agnostic drivers built on top of `embedded-hal` on crates.io by [searching
for the  embedded-hal keyword](https://crates.io/keywords/embedded-hal).

If you are writing a platform-agnostic driver yourself you are highly encouraged to [add the
embedded-hal keyword](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#package-metadata)
to your crate before publishing it!

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-cargo-features)Optional Cargo features

- `defmt-03`- `defmt::Format`from- `defmt`0.3 for enums and structs.

[§](https://docs.rs#minimum-supported-rust-version-msrv)Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust 1.60 and up. It *might*
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

See [here](https://docs.rs/docs/msrv.md) for details on how the MSRV may be upgraded.

- MIT license ([LICENSE-MIT](https://docs.rs/LICENSE-MIT)or[http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT](http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT))

at your option.

# linux_embedded_hal - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/linux-embedded-hal/^0.4/

## Expand description

Implementation of [ embedded-hal](https://docs.rs/embedded-hal) traits for Linux devices

[§](https://docs.rs#drivers)Drivers

This crate lets you use a bunch of platform agnostic drivers that are based on the
`embedded-hal` traits. You can find them on crates.io by [searching for the embedded-hal
keyword](https://crates.io/keywords/embedded-hal).

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# facett_icebergview - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-icebergview/0.1.10/facett_icebergview/

## Expand description

**facett-icebergview** — browse **and time-travel** one Iceberg table, drawn
from **Arrow  RecordBatches**. The component is

*engine-agnostic*: you hand it, per Iceberg snapshot, the snapshot’s metadata + its materialized Arrow frame; it renders a

**snapshot picker**(newest-first, showing snapshot id / timestamp / row-count) over a virtualized,

**paged**row grid (the rows come from

[, built from the batch via](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[). Selecting a snapshot loads](https://docs.rs/facett-arrow/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_arrow/index.html)

`facett_arrow`*that*snapshot’s frame — time travel.

Like every facett component it implements [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html) (

`title` / `ui` /
`state_json`), so it drops into a `FacetDeck` and is robot-testable through
`facett_core::harness`: drive [/](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.select_snapshot)

`IcebergView::select_snapshot`[headlessly and assert](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html#method.set_page)

`IcebergView::set_page``state_json` (the current snapshot, the snapshot list,
and the visible rows all change). `state_json` exposes:- `table`— the table name,
- `snapshots`— every snapshot newest-first (- `id`,- `timestamp_ms`,- `rows`),
- `current`— the selected snapshot id,
- `total_rows`/- `page`/- `page_size`/- `visible_rows`— the paged view.

**Why not just  facett-table?** A table viewer shows

*one*frame. This adds the Iceberg dimension — the history of snapshots and the control to scrub between them — which is the whole point of a lakehouse table browser. The adapter that

*fills*it from a real catalog (skade) lives host-side (korp / nornir) so this crate never takes a hard catalog/engine dependency.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Iceberg](https://docs.rs/struct.IcebergView.html)- View
- A browse + time-travel viewer for one Iceberg table.
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.Snapshot.html)
- One snapshot paired with the Arrow frame that materializes it. The frame is a
`Vec<RecordBatch>`exactly as a scan returns it;`IcebergView`concatenates the rows into a paged`Table`
- [Snapshot](https://docs.rs/struct.SnapshotMeta.html)- Meta
- One Iceberg snapshot’s identity, for the picker + `state_json`. Mirrors what`iceberg::spec::Snapshot`exposes (`snapshot_id()`/`timestamp_ms()`) plus a row count the host computes (scan count, or the snapshot summary’s`total-records`).

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE.html)- PAGE_ - SIZE
- Default rows shown per page (the Table is virtualized, but paging keeps a huge
snapshot from being cell-formatted all at once and makes `visible_rows`meaningful for headless assertions).

# facett_warehousedeck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-warehousedeck/0.1.10/facett_warehousedeck/

## Expand description

**facett-warehousedeck** — a multi-pane **dashboard over a lakehouse
warehouse**. It views the warehouse as **many components at once**: several
**3D graphs** (call graph, dependency graph, world-delta, release lineage,
SBOM/vuln) **plus** grids and charts, all visible simultaneously in a wall.

It is built **entirely from existing facett widgets** — it never reimplements
a viewer. Each pane is one of:
[ facett_graph3d::Graph3D](https://docs.rs/facett-graph3d/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_graph3d/struct.Graph3D.html) ·

[/](https://docs.rs/facett-grid/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_grid/struct.Grid.html)

`facett_grid::Grid`[·](https://docs.rs/facett-table/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_table/struct.Table.html)

`facett_table::Table`[, composed inside a](https://docs.rs/facett-plot/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_plot/struct.PlotView.html)

`facett_plot::PlotView`[. The deck is rendered in](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html)

`facett_core::FacetDeck`**Wall**mode (

[) so every pane (and thus several](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.wall_ui)

`FacetDeck::wall_ui``Graph3D` instances) draws at once; a **Focus**mode falls back to the deck’s tabbed

[.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/struct.FacetDeck.html#method.ui)

`FacetDeck::ui`[§](https://docs.rs#engine-agnostic)Engine-agnostic

Like the rest of facett, this crate takes **data, not a catalog**: a host
(nornir’s viz) opens its Iceberg warehouse, reads each table, maps the rows to
a [ PaneData](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html) view-model, and hands them in. This crate never depends on
iceberg/skade/nornir.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-registry-table--view-kind)The registry (table → view-kind)

[ WarehouseRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseRegistry.html) maps a

**table name**to the

[it should render as, so adding a table is one](https://docs.rs/enum.ViewKind.html)

`ViewKind``register(...)` line. The host queries the
registry to decide which [to build for a table; explicit join-panes (e.g. the call graph from](https://docs.rs/enum.PaneData.html)

`PaneData``call_edges`×`symbol_facts`) are added directly.[§](https://docs.rs#robot-testable)Robot-testable

[ WarehouseDeck](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html) is itself a

[, so it drops into nornir’s viz and is headless-assertable.](https://docs.rs/trait.Facet.html)

`Facet`[exposes](https://docs.rs/struct.WarehouseDeck.html#method.state_json)

`WarehouseDeck::state_json``pane_count`,
per-kind counts (`graph3d_count`, `grid_count`, …), and a `panes` array
carrying each pane’s `nodes`/`edges`/`rows`/`series`, plus the composed deck
state (whose `trace.ran` lists `deck.wall:<title>` for every pane that drew).## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-pitch-namer-riemann/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_pitch_namer_riemann/

## Expand description

Neo-Riemannian / functional triad naming for the SIM music libraries.

This crate implements the Riemannian naming school: it labels a triad by its
functional quality relative to its root, distinguishing a major triad (`T`,
upper-case for the major tonic function) from a minor triad (`t`,
lower-case). [ label_riemann](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html) rotates the pitch-class set so the root sits at
zero and matches the major or minor triad signature; non-triadic sets return

`None`.## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [label_](https://docs.rs/fn.label_riemann.html)- riemann
- Labels `mask`as a major (`T`) or minor (`t`) triad relative to its root.

# facett_security - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-security/0.1.10/facett_security/

## Expand description

**facett-security** — a software-supply-chain **security report** view: the
**verdict** (Pass / Warn / Block), the **findings** list (id · severity ·
package · advisory · fix) with **severity / EPSS / KEV** columns, and a
secondary **CVE / advisory** reference table. It is the UI *twin* of
[modgunn](https://codeberg.org/nordisk/modgunn)’s scan output — the gate that
decides whether an artifact may be served / promoted.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-on-purpose-no-modgunn-dependency)Generic on purpose (no modgunn dependency)

facett MUST NOT couple to the modgunn crate. So this crate carries its **own**
plain, serializable structs — [ Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)

`Severity`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)

`Finding`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)

`Artifact`[— whose shape](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)

`SecurityReport`**mirrors**so a consumer (nornir-viz / holger-ui) maps the two

`modgunn::core`**1:1**with no glue:

| facett-security | modgunn::core |
|---|---|
| (Pass/Warn/Block)`Verdict` | `Decision`(Pass/Warn/Block) — same`Ord` |
| (Info…Critical)`Severity` | `Severity`(Info…Critical) — same`Ord` |
| `Finding``{id,severity,…}` | `Finding``{id,severity,summary}`(superset) |
| `Artifact` | `ArtifactRef` |
| `SecurityReport` | `Verdict`(the whole cacheable result) |

[ Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html) is a

**superset**: modgunn’s three fields map straight in, and the richer scan columns the UI wants (

`package`, `advisory`, `fix`, `epss`, `kev`)
are optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has and leaves the rest defaulted.[§](https://docs.rs#fc-compliance-the-component-contract)FC compliance (the component contract)

- **FC-1 / FC-3**— all observable state lives in one serializable- `SecurityState`- `Serialize`/- `Deserialize`/- `Clone`/- `PartialEq`), read back via- `SecurityView::state`
- **FC-2 / FC-9**— every input is a- `Msg`- `SecurityView::update`- `render`- `&self`that paints and- *returns*the- `Msg`- `Facet::ui`
- **FC-4**— the painted verdict pill emits an AccessKit node; every finding row / CVE row is a selectable, labelled, value-carrying node.
- **FC-5**— rows are keyed off the finding- **id**(a stable domain key), never a loop index.
- **FC-6**— pure egui + painter, renders headlessly (the deck robot path).
- **FC-7**— no ambient clock / RNG / animation: the scan time is an- *injected*host-stamped string (- `SecurityReport::scanned_at`
- **FC-8**— the view does no I/O;- `SecurityView::is_idle`- `SecurityView::update`- `Vec<Effect>`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Artifact](https://docs.rs/struct.Artifact.html)
- The artifact a verdict is about (content-addressed). Mirrors
`modgunn::core::ArtifactRef`.
- [Finding](https://docs.rs/struct.Finding.html)
- One thing the scanner found. `id`,`severity`,`summary`map straight from`modgunn::core::Finding`; the rest are the richer scan columns the UI shows (all optional, so a 1:1 mapper fills what it has).
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityReport.html)- Report
- The cacheable scan result: the verdict + its findings + the keys it was
computed against. The plain data a host hands the view; mirrors the whole of
`modgunn::core::Verdict`.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityState.html)- State
- **All**observable state for the view (FC-1 / FC-3): the report plus the UI state (the drilled-in finding, the severity floor filter, and the zoom). Fully serializable so a caller reads it back at any frame boundary.
- [Security](https://docs.rs/struct.SecurityView.html)- View
- The `Facet``SecurityReport`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Effect](https://docs.rs/enum.Effect.html)
- Side work as data (FC-8). The view does no I/O, so this is uninhabited — it exists to make the “no pending effects” contract explicit and type-checked.
- [Msg](https://docs.rs/enum.Msg.html)
- Every input the view accepts (FC-2). The **only**legal way to mutate`SecurityState``Debug`+`Clone`.
- [Severity](https://docs.rs/enum.Severity.html)
- Finding severity (declaration order = ascending, so the worst finding is the
`max()`). Mirrors`modgunn::core::Severity`.
- [Verdict](https://docs.rs/enum.Verdict.html)
- What a gate should DO with the artifact, given the findings. Declaration
order is the strictness order — `Pass < Warn < Block`— so folding many findings into one verdict is their`Ord::max``modgunn::core::Decision`relies on).

# everruns_a2ui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-a2ui/0.17.3/everruns_a2ui/

## Expand description

A2UI component catalog and prompt generator for Everruns.

Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to emit A2UI JSON component trees. The JSON is transported in ```a2ui fenced code blocks and rendered by the UI using native shadcn/ui primitives.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_a2ui::{PromptOptions, default_catalog, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_catalog(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```a2ui"));
```
Ref: specs/a2ui.md
Ref: [https://github.com/google/a2ui](https://github.com/google/a2ui)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Catalog](https://docs.rs/struct.Catalog.html)
- A catalog describes the components an agent may emit.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentCategory.html)- Category
- One category of components in a catalog (e.g. “Layout”, “Forms”).
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentDef.html)- Def
- One component available to the agent.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptOptions.html)- Options
- Options for customizing the generated prompt.
- [PropDef](https://docs.rs/struct.PropDef.html)
- One prop of a component.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_catalog.html)- catalog
- The default A2UI catalog.
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_prompt.html)- prompt
- Generate the default A2UI system prompt with standard options.
- [generate_](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_prompt.html)- prompt
- Build the full A2UI system prompt.

# everruns_openui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/everruns-openui/0.17.3/everruns_openui/

## Expand description

OpenUI component library and prompt generator for Everruns.

Rust reimplementation of the OpenUI component definitions and prompt generator. Produces system prompts that instruct LLMs to generate OpenUI Lang code.

The generated prompt is compatible with `@openuidev/react-lang` and `@openuidev/react-ui`
— the React runtime parses the LLM output and renders it into interactive components.

This crate is part of the [Everruns](https://everruns.com) ecosystem.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use everruns_openui::{PromptOptions, default_library, generate_prompt};
let prompt = generate_prompt(default_library(), &PromptOptions::default());
assert!(prompt.contains("```openui"));
```
Ref: [https://github.com/thesysdev/openui](https://github.com/thesysdev/openui)

- Component definitions: packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib/
- Prompt generator: packages/react-lang/src/parser/prompt.ts
- Library/types: packages/react-lang/src/library.ts

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentDef.html)- Def
- A component definition.
Equivalent to TS `DefinedComponent`from`defineComponent()`.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentGroup.html)- Group
- A logical group of components for prompt organization.
- [Library](https://docs.rs/struct.Library.html)
- The full component library definition.
- [Prompt](https://docs.rs/struct.PromptOptions.html)- Options
- Options for customizing the generated prompt.
- [PropDef](https://docs.rs/struct.PropDef.html)
- A single prop/argument definition for a component.
Maps to a key in the TypeScript Zod schema’s `.shape`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_library.html)- library
- The default OpenUI library matching `@openuidev/react-ui`openuiChatLibrary. Ref: packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib/openuiChatLibrary.tsx
- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_prompt.html)- prompt
- Generate the default OpenUI system prompt with standard options.

- Generate the complete OpenUI system prompt.

# eeprom24x 0.7.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/eeprom24x/0.7.2

# Rust 24x EEPROM Driver

This is a platform agnostic Rust driver for the 24x series serial EEPROM,
based on the [ embedded-hal](https://github.com/rust-embedded/embedded-hal) traits.

This driver allows you to:

- Read a single byte from a memory address. See: `read_byte()`.
- Read a byte array starting on a memory address. See: `read_data()`.
- Read the current memory address (please read notes). See: `read_current_address()`.
- Write a byte to a memory address. See: `write_byte()`.
- Write a byte array (up to a memory page) to a memory address. See: `write_page()`.
- Read `CSx`-variant devices' factory-programmed unique serial. See:`read_unique_serial()`.
- Use the device in generic code via the `Eeprom24xTrait`.

Can be used at least with the devices listed below.

## The devices

These devices provides a number of bits of serial electrically erasable and programmable read only memory (EEPROM) organized as a number of words of 8 bits each. The devices' cascadable feature allows up to 8 devices to share a common 2-wire bus. The devices are optimized for use in many industrial and commercial applications where low power and low voltage operation are essential.

| Device | Memory bits | 8-bit words | Page size | Datasheet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24x00 | 128 bits | 16 | N/A | [24C00](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/24AA00-24LC00-24C00-Data-Sheet-20001178J.pdf) |
| 24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 8 bytes | [AT24C01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 16 bytes | [M24C01](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c01-r.pdf) |
| 24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 8 bytes | [AT24C02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 16 bytes | [M24C02](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c02-r.pdf) |
| 24x04 | 4 Kbit | 512 | 16 bytes | [AT24C04](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8896E-SEEPROM-AT24C04D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x08 | 8 Kbit | 1,024 | 16 bytes | [AT24C08](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/AT24C08D-I2C-Compatible-2-Wire-Serial-EEPROM-20006022A.pdf) |
| 24x16 | 16 Kbit | 2,048 | 16 bytes | [AT24C16](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/20005858A.pdf) |
| 24x32 | 32 Kbit | 4,096 | 32 bytes | [AT24C32](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x64 | 64 Kbit | 8,192 | 32 bytes | [AT24C64](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x128 | 128 Kbit | 16,384 | 64 bytes | [AT24C128](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8734-SEEPROM-AT24C128C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x256 | 256 Kbit | 32,768 | 64 bytes | [AT24C256](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8568-SEEPROM-AT24C256C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x512 | 512 Kbit | 65,536 | 128 bytes | [AT24C512](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8720-SEEPROM-AT24C512C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM01 | 1 Mbit | 131,072 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8812-SEEPROM-AT24CM01-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM02 | 2 Mbit | 262,144 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8828-SEEPROM-AT24CM02-Datasheet.pdf) |

## Usage

To use this driver, import this crate and an `embedded_hal` implementation,
then instantiate the appropriate device.
In the following examples an instance of the device AT24C256 will be created
as an example. Other devices can be created with similar methods like:
`Eeprom24x::new_24x64(...)`.

Please find additional examples using hardware in this repository: [driver-examples](https://github.com/eldruin/driver-examples)

```
use ;
use DelayMs;
use ;
```
## Features

### defmt-03

To enable [defmt](https://crates.io/crates/defmt) (version `0.3.x`) support, when specifying the dependency on `eeprom24x`, add the feature "`defmt-03`".

```
[]
 = {  = "0.7.2",  = ["defmt-03"] }
```

For questions, issues, feature requests, and other changes, please file an
[issue in the github project](https://github.com/eldruin/eeprom24x-rs/issues).

# eeprom24x - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/eeprom24x/0.7.2/target-redirect/eeprom24x/

## Expand description

This is a platform agnostic Rust driver for the 24x series serial EEPROM,
based on the [ embedded-hal](https://github.com/rust-embedded/embedded-hal) traits.

This driver allows you to:

- Read a single byte from a memory address. See `read_byte()`
- Read a byte array starting on a memory address. See: `read_data()`
- Read the current memory address (please read notes). See: `read_current_address()`
- Write a byte to a memory address. See: `write_byte()`
- Write a byte array (up to a memory page) to a memory address. See: `write_page()`
- Read `CSx`-variant devices’ factory-programmed unique serial. See:`read_unique_serial()`
- Use the device in generic code via the `Eeprom24xTrait`

If an `embedded_hal::timer::CountDown` is available, the [ embedded-storage](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/embedded-storage) traits can
additionally be used which allow to read the device capacity and write over page boundaries. To
achieve the latter, the

[has to be wrapped with](https://docs.rs/struct.Eeprom24x.html)

`Eeprom24x`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Storage.html#method.new)

`Storage::new`Can be used at least with the devices listed below.

[§](https://docs.rs#the-devices)The devices

These devices provides a number of bits of serial electrically erasable and programmable read only memory (EEPROM) organized as a number of words of 8 bits each. The devices’ cascadable feature allows up to 8 devices to share a common 2-wire bus. The devices are optimized for use in many industrial and commercial applications where low power and low voltage operation are essential.

| Device | Memory bits | 8-bit words | Page size | Datasheet |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 24x00 | 128 bits | 16 | N/A | [24C00](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/24AA00-24LC00-24C00-Data-Sheet-20001178J.pdf) |
| 24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 8 bytes | [AT24C01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x01 | 1 Kbit | 128 | 16 bytes | [M24C01](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c01-r.pdf) |
| 24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 8 bytes | [AT24C02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| M24x02 | 2 Kbit | 256 | 16 bytes | [M24C02](https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c02-r.pdf) |
| 24x04 | 4 Kbit | 512 | 16 bytes | [AT24C04](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8896E-SEEPROM-AT24C04D-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x08 | 8 Kbit | 1,024 | 16 bytes | [AT24C08](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/AT24C08D-I2C-Compatible-2-Wire-Serial-EEPROM-20006022A.pdf) |
| 24x16 | 16 Kbit | 2,048 | 16 bytes | [AT24C16](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/20005858A.pdf) |
| 24x32 | 32 Kbit | 4,096 | 32 bytes | [AT24C32](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x64 | 64 Kbit | 8,192 | 32 bytes | [AT24C64](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf) |
| 24x128 | 128 Kbit | 16,384 | 64 bytes | [AT24C128](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8734-SEEPROM-AT24C128C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x256 | 256 Kbit | 32,768 | 64 bytes | [AT24C256](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8568-SEEPROM-AT24C256C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24x512 | 512 Kbit | 65,536 | 128 bytes | [AT24C512](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8720-SEEPROM-AT24C512C-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM01 | 1 Mbit | 131,072 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM01](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8812-SEEPROM-AT24CM01-Datasheet.pdf) |
| 24xM02 | 2 Mbit | 262,144 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM02](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8828-SEEPROM-AT24CM02-Datasheet.pdf) |

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

[§](https://docs.rs#defmt-03)defmt-03

To enable [defmt](https://crates.io/crates/defmt) (version `0.3.x`) support, when specifying the dependency on `eeprom24x`, add the feature “`defmt-03`”.

```
[dependencies]
eeprom24x = { version = "0.7.2", features = ["defmt-03"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#usage-examples-see-also-examples-folder)Usage examples (see also examples folder)

To create a new instance you can use the `new_<device>` methods.
There are many compatible vendors so the method has a somewhat generic name.
For example, if you are using an AT24C32, you can create a device by calling
`Eeprom24x::new_24x32(...)`.
Please refer to the [device table](https://docs.rs#the-devices) above for further examples
of device names.

Please find additional examples using hardware in this repository: [driver-examples](https://github.com/eldruin/driver-examples)

[§](https://docs.rs#instantiating-with-the-default-address)Instantiating with the default address

Import this crate and an `embedded_hal` implementation, then instantiate
the device:

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let address = SlaveAddr::default();
// using the AT24C256
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, address);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#providing-an-alternative-address)Providing an alternative address

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let (a2, a1, a0) = (false, false, true);
let address = SlaveAddr::Alternative(a2, a1, a0);
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, address);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#writing-and-reading-a-byte)Writing and reading a byte

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
let address = 0x1234;
let data = 0xAB;
eeprom.write_byte(address, data);
// EEPROM enters internally-timed write cycle. Will not respond for some time.
let retrieved_data = eeprom.read_byte(address);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#writing-a-page)Writing a page

```
use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
let address = 0x1234;
let data = [0xAB; 64];
eeprom.write_page(address, &data);
// EEPROM enters internally-timed write cycle. Will not respond for some time.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-embedded-storage-traits)Using embedded-storage traits

```
use linux_embedded_hal::{I2cdev, Delay};
use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr, Storage };
use embedded_storage::{ReadStorage, Storage as _};
let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
let eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
let mut storage = Storage::new(eeprom, Delay {});
let _capacity = storage.capacity();
let address = 0x1234;
let data = [0xAB; 256];
storage.write(address, &data);
// EEPROM writes four pages. This introduces a delay of at least 20 ms, 5 ms per page.
```

- [addr_](https://docs.rs/addr_size/index.html)- size
- Memory address size markers
- [page_](https://docs.rs/page_size/index.html)- size
- Page size markers
- [unique_](https://docs.rs/unique_serial/index.html)- serial

- EEPROM24X extension which supports the `embedded-storage`traits but requires an`embedded_hal::delay::DelayNs`to handle the timeouts when writing over page boundaries

# eeprom24x/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! This is a platform agnostic Rust driver for the 24x series serial EEPROM,
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! based on the [`embedded-hal`] traits.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! [`embedded-hal`]: https://github.com/rust-embedded/embedded-hal
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! This driver allows you to:
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! - Read a single byte from a memory address. See [`read_byte()`].
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! - Read a byte array starting on a memory address. See: [`read_data()`].
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! - Read the current memory address (please read notes). See: [`read_current_address()`].
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! - Write a byte to a memory address. See: [`write_byte()`].
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! - Write a byte array (up to a memory page) to a memory address. See: [`write_page()`].
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! - Read `CSx`-variant devices' factory-programmed unique serial. See: [`read_unique_serial()`].
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! - Use the device in generic code via the [`Eeprom24xTrait`].
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! [`read_byte()`]: Eeprom24x::read_byte
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! [`read_data()`]: Eeprom24x::read_data
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! [`read_current_address()`]: Eeprom24x::read_current_address
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! [`write_byte()`]: Eeprom24x::write_byte
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! [`write_page()`]: Eeprom24x::write_page
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! [`read_unique_serial()`]: Eeprom24x::read_unique_serial
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! [`Eeprom24xTrait`]: Eeprom24xTrait
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! If an `embedded_hal::timer::CountDown` is available, the [`embedded-storage`] traits can
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! additionally be used which allow to read the device capacity and write over page boundaries. To
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! achieve the latter, the [`Eeprom24x`] has to be wrapped with [`Storage::new`].
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! [`embedded-storage`]: https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/embedded-storage
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! Can be used at least with the devices listed below.
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! ## The devices
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! These devices provides a number of bits of serial electrically erasable and
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! programmable read only memory (EEPROM) organized as a number of words of 8 bits
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//! each. The devices' cascadable feature allows up to 8 devices to share a common
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! 2-wire bus. The devices are optimized for use in many industrial and commercial
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! applications where low power and low voltage operation are essential.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! | Device | Memory bits | 8-bit words | Page size | Datasheet  |
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! |-------:|------------:|------------:|----------:|:-----------|
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! |  24x00 |    128 bits |          16 |       N/A | [24C00]    |
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! |  24x01 |      1 Kbit |         128 |   8 bytes | [AT24C01]  |
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! | M24x01 |      1 Kbit |         128 |  16 bytes | [M24C01]   |
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! |  24x02 |      2 Kbit |         256 |   8 bytes | [AT24C02]  |
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! | M24x02 |      2 Kbit |         256 |  16 bytes | [M24C02]   |
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! |  24x04 |      4 Kbit |         512 |  16 bytes | [AT24C04]  |
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! |  24x08 |      8 Kbit |       1,024 |  16 bytes | [AT24C08]  |
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! |  24x16 |     16 Kbit |       2,048 |  16 bytes | [AT24C16]  |
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! |  24x32 |     32 Kbit |       4,096 |  32 bytes | [AT24C32]  |
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! |  24x64 |     64 Kbit |       8,192 |  32 bytes | [AT24C64]  |
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! | 24x128 |    128 Kbit |      16,384 |  64 bytes | [AT24C128] |
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! | 24x256 |    256 Kbit |      32,768 |  64 bytes | [AT24C256] |
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! | 24x512 |    512 Kbit |      65,536 | 128 bytes | [AT24C512] |
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! | 24xM01 |      1 Mbit |     131,072 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM01] |
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! | 24xM02 |      2 Mbit |     262,144 | 256 bytes | [AT24CM02] |
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! [24C00]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/24AA00-24LC00-24C00-Data-Sheet-20001178J.pdf
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! [AT24C01]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! [M24C01]: https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c01-r.pdf
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! [AT24C02]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8871F-SEEPROM-AT24C01D-02D-Datasheet.pdf
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! [M24C02]: https://www.st.com/resource/en/datasheet/m24c02-r.pdf
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! [AT24C04]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8896E-SEEPROM-AT24C04D-Datasheet.pdf
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! [AT24C08]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/AT24C08D-I2C-Compatible-2-Wire-Serial-EEPROM-20006022A.pdf
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! [AT24C16]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/20005858A.pdf
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! [AT24C32]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! [AT24C64]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/devicedoc/doc0336.pdf
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! [AT24C128]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8734-SEEPROM-AT24C128C-Datasheet.pdf
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! [AT24C256]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8568-SEEPROM-AT24C256C-Datasheet.pdf
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! [AT24C512]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8720-SEEPROM-AT24C512C-Datasheet.pdf
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! [AT24CM01]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8812-SEEPROM-AT24CM01-Datasheet.pdf
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! [AT24CM02]: https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/Atmel-8828-SEEPROM-AT24CM02-Datasheet.pdf
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! ## Features
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! ### defmt-03
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! To enable [defmt](https://crates.io/crates/defmt) (version `0.3.x`) support, when specifying the dependency on `eeprom24x`, add the feature "`defmt-03`".
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//! ```toml
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! [dependencies]
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! eeprom24x = { version = "0.7.2", features = ["defmt-03"] }
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! ```
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ## Usage examples (see also examples folder)
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! To create a new instance you can use the `new_<device>` methods.
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! There are many compatible vendors so the method has a somewhat generic name.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! For example, if you are using an AT24C32, you can create a device by calling
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! `Eeprom24x::new_24x32(...)`.
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! Please refer to the [device table](#the-devices) above for further examples
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! of device names.
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! Please find additional examples using hardware in this repository: [driver-examples]
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! [driver-examples]: https://github.com/eldruin/driver-examples
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! ### Instantiating with the default address
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! Import this crate and an `embedded_hal` implementation, then instantiate
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! the device:
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ```no_run
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! let address = SlaveAddr::default();
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! // using the AT24C256
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, address);
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! ```
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! ### Providing an alternative address
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! ```no_run
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! # fn main() {
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! let (a2, a1, a0) = (false, false, true);
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! let address = SlaveAddr::Alternative(a2, a1, a0);
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, address);
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! # }
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! ```
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! ### Writing and reading a byte
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! ```no_run
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//! use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! let address = 0x1234;
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! let data = 0xAB;
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! eeprom.write_byte(address, data);
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! // EEPROM enters internally-timed write cycle. Will not respond for some time.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//! let retrieved_data = eeprom.read_byte(address);
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! ```
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! ### Writing a page
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! ```no_run
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! use linux_embedded_hal::I2cdev;
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr };
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! let mut eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! let address = 0x1234;
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! let data = [0xAB; 64];
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! eeprom.write_page(address, &data);
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! // EEPROM enters internally-timed write cycle. Will not respond for some time.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! ```
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! ### Using embedded-storage traits
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! ```no_run
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! use linux_embedded_hal::{I2cdev, Delay};
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! use eeprom24x::{ Eeprom24x, SlaveAddr, Storage };
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! use embedded_storage::{ReadStorage, Storage as _};
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! let dev = I2cdev::new("/dev/i2c-1").unwrap();
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! let eeprom = Eeprom24x::new_24x256(dev, SlaveAddr::default());
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! let mut storage = Storage::new(eeprom, Delay {});
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! let _capacity = storage.capacity();
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! let address = 0x1234;
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! let data = [0xAB; 256];
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! storage.write(address, &data);
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! // EEPROM writes four pages. This introduces a delay of at least 20 ms, 5 ms per page.
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! ```
[171](https://docs.rs#171)
[172](https://docs.rs#172)#![deny(missing_docs, unsafe_code)]
[173](https://docs.rs#173)#![no_std]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)use core::marker::PhantomData;
[176](https://docs.rs#176)
[177](https://docs.rs#177)/// All possible errors in this crate
[178](https://docs.rs#178)#[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[179](https://docs.rs#179)#[derive(Debug)]
[180](https://docs.rs#180)pub enum Error<E> {
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// I²C bus error
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    I2C(E),
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    /// Too much data passed for a write
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    TooMuchData,
[185](https://docs.rs#185)    /// Memory address is out of range
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    InvalidAddr,
[187](https://docs.rs#187)}
[188](https://docs.rs#188)
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// Possible slave addresses
[190](https://docs.rs#190)///
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// Note that in some devices some of the address bits are used for memory addressing and
[192](https://docs.rs#192)/// will therefore be ignored.
[193](https://docs.rs#193)#[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[194](https://docs.rs#194)#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq)]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)pub enum SlaveAddr {
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// Default slave address
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    Default,
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// Alternative slave address providing bit values for A2, A1 and A0
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    ///
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// Depending on the device, some of the device address bits may be used for memory addresses.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// In this case, the value provided here for these bits will be ignored. Consult the
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// device addressing in your device datasheet.
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    ///
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// e.g. For the 24xM01 devices use the A0 bit of the device address as the highest memory
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    /// address bit. The value provided here will be ignored.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    Alternative(bool, bool, bool),
[207](https://docs.rs#207)}
[208](https://docs.rs#208)
[209](https://docs.rs#209)/// Memory address size markers
[210](https://docs.rs#210)pub mod addr_size {
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// 1-byte memory address.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// e.g. for AT24x00, AT24x01, AT24x02, AT24x04, AT24x08, AT24x16
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    #[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    #[derive(Debug)]
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    pub struct OneByte(());
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// 2-byte memory address.
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    /// e.g. for AT24x32, AT24x64, AT24x128, AT24x256, AT24x512, AT24xM01, AT24xM02
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    #[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    #[derive(Debug)]
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    pub struct TwoBytes(());
[221](https://docs.rs#221)}

[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// 16-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x04, AT24x08, AT24x16

[235](https://docs.rs#235)    #[derive(Debug)]

[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// 32-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x32, AT24x64

[239](https://docs.rs#239)    #[derive(Debug)]
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    pub struct B32(());
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    /// 64-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x128, AT24x256
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    #[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    #[derive(Debug)]
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    pub struct B64(());
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// 128-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x512
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    #[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    #[derive(Debug)]
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    pub struct B128(());
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    /// 256-byte pages. e.g. for AT24xM01, AT24xM02

[267](https://docs.rs#267)/// EEPROM24X driver
[268](https://docs.rs#268)#[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[269](https://docs.rs#269)#[derive(Debug)]
[270](https://docs.rs#270)pub struct Eeprom24x<I2C, PS, AS, SN> {
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// The concrete I²C device implementation.
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    i2c: I2C,
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// The I²C device address.
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    address: SlaveAddr,
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    /// Number or bits used for memory addressing.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    address_bits: u8,
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// Page size marker type.
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    _ps: PhantomData<PS>,
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// Address size marker type.
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    _as: PhantomData<AS>,
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// Unique serial number marker type.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    _sn: PhantomData<SN>,
[283](https://docs.rs#283)}
[284](https://docs.rs#284)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// `Eeprom24x` type trait for use in generic code
[286](https://docs.rs#286)pub trait Eeprom24xTrait: private::Sealed {
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    /// Inner implementation error.
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    type Error;
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// Write a single byte in an address.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    ///
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// After writing a byte, the EEPROM enters an internally-timed write cycle
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    /// to the nonvolatile memory.
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    /// During this time all inputs are disabled and the EEPROM will not
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    /// respond until the write is complete.
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    fn write_byte(&mut self, address: u32, data: u8) -> Result<(), Error<Self::Error>>;
[297](https://docs.rs#297)
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// Read a single byte from an address.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    fn read_byte(&mut self, address: u32) -> Result<u8, Error<Self::Error>>;
[300](https://docs.rs#300)
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// Read starting in an address as many bytes as necessary to fill the data array provided.
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    fn read_data(&mut self, address: u32, data: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Error<Self::Error>>;
[303](https://docs.rs#303)
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    /// Read the contents of the last address accessed during the last read
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// or write operation, _incremented by one_.
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    ///
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    /// Note: This may not be available on your platform.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    fn read_current_address(&mut self) -> Result<u8, Error<Self::Error>>;
[309](https://docs.rs#309)
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    /// Write up to a page starting in an address.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    ///
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// The maximum amount of data that can be written depends on the page
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// size of the device and its overall capacity. If too much data is passed,
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// the error `Error::TooMuchData` will be returned.
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    ///
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    /// After writing a byte, the EEPROM enters an internally-timed write cycle
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// to the nonvolatile memory.
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    /// During this time all inputs are disabled and the EEPROM will not
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    /// respond until the write is complete.
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    fn write_page(&mut self, address: u32, data: &[u8]) -> Result<(), Error<Self::Error>>;
[321](https://docs.rs#321)
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// Return device page size
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    fn page_size(&self) -> usize;
[324](https://docs.rs#324)}
[325](https://docs.rs#325)
[326](https://docs.rs#326)/// EEPROM24X extension which supports the `embedded-storage` traits but requires an
[327](https://docs.rs#327)/// `embedded_hal::delay::DelayNs` to handle the timeouts when writing over page boundaries
[328](https://docs.rs#328)#[cfg_attr(feature = "defmt-03", derive(defmt::Format))]
[329](https://docs.rs#329)#[derive(Debug)]

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Write a single byte in an address.

After writing a byte, the EEPROM enters an internally-timed write cycle to the nonvolatile memory. During this time all inputs are disabled and the EEPROM will not respond until the write is complete.

}## Expand description

`Eeprom24x` type trait for use in generic code

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Write a single byte in an address.

After writing a byte, the EEPROM enters an internally-timed write cycle to the nonvolatile memory. During this time all inputs are disabled and the EEPROM will not respond until the write is complete.

Read a single byte from an address.

Read starting in an address as many bytes as necessary to fill the data array provided.

Read the contents of the last address accessed during the last read
or write operation, *incremented by one*.

Note: This may not be available on your platform.

Write up to a page starting in an address.

The maximum amount of data that can be written depends on the page
size of the device and its overall capacity. If too much data is passed,
the error `Error::TooMuchData` will be returned.

After writing a byte, the EEPROM enters an internally-timed write cycle to the nonvolatile memory. During this time all inputs are disabled and the EEPROM will not respond until the write is complete.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# eeprom24x::page_size - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eeprom24x/0.7.2/eeprom24x/page_size/index.html

## Expand description

Page size markers

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [B8](https://docs.rs/struct.B8.html)
- 8-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x01, AT24x02
- [B16](https://docs.rs/struct.B16.html)
- 16-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x04, AT24x08, AT24x16
- [B32](https://docs.rs/struct.B32.html)
- 32-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x32, AT24x64
- [B64](https://docs.rs/struct.B64.html)
- 64-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x128, AT24x256
- [B128](https://docs.rs/struct.B128.html)
- 128-byte pages. e.g. for AT24x512
- [B256](https://docs.rs/struct.B256.html)
- 256-byte pages. e.g. for AT24xM01, AT24xM02
- [No](https://docs.rs/struct.No.html)
- No page write supported. e.g. for AT24x00

# SlaveAddr in eeprom24x - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/eeprom24x/0.7.2/eeprom24x/enum.SlaveAddr.html

## Expand description

Possible slave addresses

Note that in some devices some of the address bits are used for memory addressing and will therefore be ignored.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Default)

### Default

Default slave address

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Alternative)

Alternative slave address providing bit values for A2, A1 and A0

Depending on the device, some of the device address bits may be used for memory addresses. In this case, the value provided here for these bits will be ignored. Consult the device addressing in your device datasheet.

e.g. For the 24xM01 devices use the A0 bit of the device address as the highest memory address bit. The value provided here will be ignored.
